name: AutoMQ
workload: OpenMessaging-benchmark-style 1-topic/1000-partitions/4KB messages at fixed producer rates (128000 msg/s and 25600 msg/s) run repeatedly in CI against AutoMQ, Apache Kafka, and AWS MSK clusters on identical topic/producer/consumer configs.
claimed_speedup: Pub Latency avg 3.4ms vs Kafka 4.2ms, P99 15.19ms vs 30.21ms in one run (similarly ~14-16ms vs 37-40ms P99 in other runs); at 100MB/s rate: 8.08ms avg / 30.62ms P99 vs Kafka 17.98ms / 75.13ms. Throughput itself was pinned equal (~500MB/s) by the fixed producer rate; AutoMQ also reported far lower total cost (e.g. $2373 vs $10647) at equal throughput.
hardware: AWS EC2 (specific instance types not stated in the issue thread; replicationFactor AutoMQ=1, Kafka=3)
tradeoffs: AutoMQ is a diskless Kafka-protocol-compatible broker backed by S3; lower replication factor (1 vs Kafka's 3) reduces write durability model even though data lands on S3; results are self-reported CI runs by the AutoMQ team, not run by a neutral third party.
caveats: Benchmark repo (AutoMQ/kafka-provider-comparison) is first-party (AutoMQ-authored), last commit 2024-07-12 (stale/abandoned as a comparison tool even though AutoMQ itself is active); exact CPU/instance model not stated in the issue; throughput was capped by producerRate so it isn't a throughput-speedup claim, only latency/cost.

name: Apache Pulsar
workload: OpenMessaging Benchmark-style test on 3 broker VMs (i3en.6xlarge) + 4 client VMs (m5n.8xlarge) on AWS: max throughput with 100 partitions, publish latency at a fixed 500MB/s rate, and catch-up read throughput draining a 512GB backlog.
claimed_speedup: Max throughput: Pulsar (no journaling) 1600MB/s vs Kafka 1087MB/s (~2.5x); Pulsar with journaling 800MB/s. P99 publish latency at 500MB/s: Pulsar (no journaling) 1.58ms vs Kafka 3.46ms (Pulsar with journaling 7.89ms). Catch-up read throughput: Pulsar ~3.2GB/s vs Kafka ~2.0GB/s. StreamNative also claims '100x lower' P99.99 publish latency in one scenario.
hardware: 3x i3en.6xlarge brokers (24-core, 192GB RAM, 25Gbps, dual NVMe SSD), 4x m5n.8xlarge clients (32-core, 128GB RAM, 25Gbps), t2.small ZooKeeper nodes
tradeoffs: Pulsar's 'no journaling' fastest mode trades some durability guarantees; Pulsar has a more complex operational footprint (separate Broker + BookKeeper + ZooKeeper) than Kafka; JVM-based, so no compiler/flags apply.
caveats: Benchmark is run and published by StreamNative, the company founded by Pulsar's creators — a first-party, vendor-interested comparison, not an independent third party, despite detailed hardware/workload disclosure. Hardware given as AWS instance types, not raw CPU model.

name: Apache Fluss
workload: rednote (Xiaohongshu) production migration of a real-time search/recommendation/ads indexing pipeline (a single table ingesting ~1 billion records / 10TB per day) from Kafka to Fluss, using column pruning and tiered storage.
claimed_speedup: ~3x peak throughput increase and 30-90% lower bandwidth usage on online workloads after migrating from Kafka; write-path CPU usage down ~30% and write traffic down ~50%; batch/incremental index builds 50-80% faster.
tradeoffs: Fluss is columnar streaming storage designed around Flink/lakehouse integration (Paimon tiering), not a drop-in Kafka replacement API-wise; gains are workload-specific (wide tables with many column-selective consumers) rather than general-purpose.
caveats: First-party case study published on the Fluss project's own blog citing an end-user's self-reported production numbers; no absolute throughput figures, hardware, or independent methodology given, only relative percentages/multipliers.
